blocks.text: Retrieval augmented generation, RAG for short, is a simple idea with a big payoff. Instead of asking a model to answer purely from what it memorized during training, you fetch relevant information first and hand it to the model as context.
MCP turns out to be a natural fit for building RAG pipelines, because retrieval is exactly the kind of external action that tools and resources were designed to standardize.

This topic walks through the RAG pattern itself, how MCP tools and resources map onto its two steps, and what changes once retrieval lives behind an MCP server instead of being written straight into your application.
1. What Retrieval Augmented Generation Actually Is
RAG is a two step pattern. First you retrieve a small set of relevant documents or passages, then you generate an answer that is grounded in what you retrieved.
The model never has to know something in advance. It only has to read well and reason well over whatever was handed to it.
This is different from fine tuning, which bakes knowledge into the model weights and requires retraining every time the underlying facts change.
RAG keeps the model frozen and swaps out the knowledge instead, which is much cheaper and much faster to update.

items: Retrieve, find the documents most relevant to the question
Generate, answer using the retrieved documents as context
Repeat, fresh retrieval on every new question, no retraining required

blocks.text: 2. Why RAG Exists: The Limits of Model Knowledge
Every language model has a knowledge cutoff and a fixed set of facts baked in during training.
It also has no idea about your private documents, your internal wiki, or last night’s support tickets, unless someone puts that content in front of it.
RAG solves both problems at once by fetching fresh, private, or simply forgotten information right before the model answers.
It also gives you a cheap form of citation. If you know which chunk an answer came from, you can show the user exactly where it came from.
That traceability is often just as valuable as the accuracy gain, especially in support, legal, or medical settings.
3. The Two Step Pattern: Retrieve, Then Generate

blocks.alt: The Two Step Pattern: Retrieve, Then Generate
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441306674-139995688.png
The retrieve step usually means embedding the user’s question into a vector and finding the nearest neighbors in a vector database.
The generate step takes those neighbors, stitches them into a prompt alongside the original question, and asks the model to answer using only that material.
Nothing about this pattern requires MCP specifically, it works with any plumbing that can move text from a database into a prompt.

blocks.title: Why order matters
blocks.content: Retrieval has to finish before generation starts. The model does not fetch its own context mid answer unless it is explicitly given a tool for that.

blocks.text: 4. Where MCP Fits Into a RAG Pipeline
MCP gives you two building blocks that map directly onto the two steps of RAG, tools for the retrieve step, and resources for reading a full document once you know which one you want.
Instead of writing custom retrieval code inside every agent that needs it, you expose retrieval once, as an MCP server, and any MCP aware client can use it.
The agent’s reasoning loop stays exactly the same, only the origin of the retrieved context changes.
This is the same separation of concerns that makes MCP useful everywhere else, the model decides when to retrieve, MCP decides how the retrieval actually happens.
5. MCP Tools as the Retrieval Step

blocks.alt: MCP Tools as the Retrieval Step
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441306675-725993335.png
A search tool is the natural MCP shape for retrieval. It takes a query string, and maybe a few filters, and returns a list of candidate chunks with their scores.
Because it is a tool, the model decides when to call it. A question that needs no outside knowledge can skip retrieval entirely.
A good tool description matters here more than usual, it should say plainly that this tool must be called before answering questions about internal or private content.
6. MCP Resources as Full Document Access

blocks.alt: MCP Resources as Full Document Access
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441306941-57971547.png

Resources are MCP’s answer to reading something whole. Once the agent knows a document’s identifier from a search result, it can request the resource directly instead of trying to reconstruct the full text from a handful of chunks.
This keeps the two steps honest, search returns compact matches for deciding what to read, resources return the complete thing when the model actually needs it.
A resource is usually addressed by a simple identifier, something like a document id or a uri, and it returns the raw text of that one document.
7. An MCP Server Wrapping a Vector Database

blocks.alt: An MCP Server Wrapping a Vector Database
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441306943-957763703.png
Building this server is mostly plumbing, take a query, embed it the same way your documents were embedded, run a similarity search, and format the top results as a tool response.
The server owns the embedding model, the index, and the connection details. None of that ever needs to leak into the agent.
The same server can expose both halves of the pattern at once, a search_docs tool for retrieval and a read_document resource for full text access.

code.content:
from mcp.server import Server
import mcp.types as types
import json

app = Server("knowledge-base-server")
vector_db = connect_to_vector_db()
embed = load_embedding_model()

@app.call_tool()
async def search_docs(name: str, arguments: dict) -> list[types.TextContent]:
    query_vector = embed(arguments["query"])
    top_k = arguments.get("top_k", 5)
    hits = vector_db.similarity_search(query_vector, k=top_k)

    results = [
        {"text": hit.chunk_text, "source": hit.document_id, "score": hit.score}
        for hit in hits
    ]
    return [types.TextContent(type="text", text=json.dumps(results))]

@app.read_resource()
async def read_document(uri: str) -> str:
    document_id = uri.removeprefix("docs://")
    return document_store.get_full_text(document_id)

blocks.text: 8. A Closer Look at the Search Tool Code
The embedding step has to use the same model that embedded the documents in the first place, otherwise the query vector and the document vectors will not live in a comparable space.
The result includes the source document id alongside the chunk text, so the agent can later call read_document if it needs the surrounding context.
Returning a score with every chunk lets the agent, or the prompt building code around it, decide how many results are actually worth keeping.
9. Chunking and Why It Matters for Retrieval
Documents get split into overlapping chunks before they are embedded, because a whole document is usually too big and too unfocused to match well against a short question.
Chunk size is a real design decision. Too small and you lose context, too large and irrelevant text dilutes the match.
Overlap between neighboring chunks helps too, it reduces the odds that the one sentence you actually need got cut right at a chunk boundary.

blocks.text: 10. Grounding the Generation Step
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441306944-252308575.png
Once chunks come back from the tool call, the agent’s job is to place them into the prompt clearly, usually with a short instruction to answer only from the provided material.
Grounding also means telling the model what to do when the retrieved chunks do not actually answer the question, rather than letting it guess.
A well grounded prompt also asks the model to point to which chunk it used, which makes the whole answer easier to check afterward.

blocks.title: Say so when nothing matches
blocks.content: If the retrieved chunks do not actually answer the question, the prompt should tell the model to say that plainly instead of filling the gap with a guess.

blocks.text: 11. MCP Based Retrieval vs a Hardcoded RAG Pipeline

blocks.alt: MCP Based Retrieval vs a Hardcoded RAG Pipeline
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441306944-587850887.png
A hardcoded RAG pipeline wires the vector database client directly into the application. The retrieval code, the embedding model, and the prompt assembly all live in one codebase.
MCP based retrieval moves that same logic behind a server boundary, so any MCP client, not just your own application, can call the same search tool the same way.
The practical difference shows up the moment you want to reuse retrieval somewhere else, swap the underlying database, or let a different agent framework use the same knowledge base.
A hardcoded pipeline is not wrong, it is often the simplest choice for a single application that will never need to share its retrieval logic.

blocks.text: 12. Composability: Swapping Sources Without Touching the Agent

blocks.alt: Composability: Swapping Sources Without Touching the Agent
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441306945-696880586.png
Because the agent only ever sees a tool named something like search_docs, the vector database behind it can change providers entirely without a single line of agent code changing.
The same idea applies to adding a second knowledge base. You expose it as another MCP server, and the agent can call whichever one is relevant.
This is what lets a single agent framework serve many teams, each team’s knowledge base is just another MCP server on the list.
13. Failure Modes Specific to MCP Based RAG
Latency compounds. A tool call over MCP adds a network hop that a direct in process function call does not have, so a slow server makes the whole loop feel sluggish.
Schema drift is another risk. If the server changes what a search result looks like without warning, every client that consumes it can break at once.
Silent low quality retrieval is the sneakiest failure of all, the call succeeds, chunks come back, but they are the wrong chunks, and the model answers confidently from bad context.
None of these are unique to MCP, they are the ordinary cost of putting a network boundary between two things that used to be one function call.

blocks.title: Watch retrieval quality, not just uptime
blocks.content: A search tool that returns fast and never errors can still be failing quietly if the chunks it returns are the wrong ones. Log what gets retrieved, not just whether the call succeeded.

blocks.text: 14. Worked Example
Say a support agent needs to answer a question about a refund policy that changed last month.
The agent calls the search_docs tool with the user’s question, and gets back three chunks from the refund policy page.
One chunk mentions an updated window but not the exact date, so the agent calls read_document on that same source to check the effective date directly.
It then answers using only that retrieved text, and states the effective date explicitly, instead of relying on whatever refund rules it happened to memorize during training.
15. Common Mistakes
A few mistakes show up again and again once retrieval moves behind an MCP server.
Most of them are easy to spot once you know to look for them.

items: Skipping the resource step and trying to answer from tiny chunks alone when the full document was actually needed
Letting the search tool return too many chunks, which drowns the real answer in noise
Not grounding the prompt, so the model blends retrieved text with its own memorized guesses
Treating a slow or failing MCP server as if it were a local function call with no error handling
Never re embedding documents after they change, so the vector database quietly goes stale

blocks.text: 16. Practice
Try wrapping a small folder of markdown files as an MCP server, one tool for search and one resource per file for full reads.
Ask a handful of questions you already know the answer to, and check what the search tool actually returned before the model answered.
Then try breaking it on purpose, shrink top_k to one and see how often the answer gets worse.

items: Pick ten to twenty short markdown files as your knowledge base
Chunk each file and embed the chunks into a small vector store
Write a search_docs tool that embeds the query and returns the top matches
Write a resource handler that returns a full file by its identifier
Ask a question, inspect the retrieved chunks, then read the final answer

blocks.text: 17. Key Takeaway
RAG is retrieval followed by grounded generation, and MCP is a clean way to expose that retrieval as a tool and a resource instead of hardcoding it into one application.
The pipeline you get is one any MCP client can reuse, swap, and reason about the same way, which is the real advantage over folding retrieval straight into a single codebase.
